questions.body: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: Combination of a function bundled with references to its surrounding lexical state.

options.text: A function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment.
options.explanation: A closure gives an inner function access to an outer function's scope even after the outer function has returned and finished executing.

options.text: A method to terminate an infinite loop or background worker.
options.explanation: Closures are lexical scope bindings, not process termination hooks.

options.text: A private class member declared using the `#` symbol in ES2022.
options.explanation: Private fields are language syntax; closures are fundamental lexical scope mechanisms.

options.text: An immediately invoked function expression that deletes all global variables.
options.explanation: An IIFE creates a scope, but a closure is the combination of function and lexical environment.

questions.body: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) in JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: Period between entering block scope and variable declaration where let/const cannot be accessed.

options.text: The time period between entering a scope and the variable declaration being evaluated where accessing a `let` or `const` variable throws a ReferenceError.
options.explanation: Variables declared with `let` and `const` are hoisted to the top of the block, but remain uninitialized in the TDZ until the execution thread evaluates the declaration.

options.text: The delay between an asynchronous HTTP fetch and promise resolution.
options.explanation: TDZ is purely a lexical scope variable initialization phenomenon.

options.text: The duration an object sits in the heap before garbage collection sweeps it.
options.explanation: That describes GC lifecycle, not TDZ.

options.text: The period where global `var` variables are undefined during script loading.
options.explanation: `var` is initialized to `undefined` upon hoisting, so it has no TDZ.

questions.keyPoints: var has function scope; by the time setTimeout callbacks execute, i has reached 3.

options.explanation: `var` is function-scoped (or global). All three timeout callbacks close over the exact same variable `i`, which equals `3` when the event loop executes the timer queue.
`0, 1, 2` would occur if `let i = 0` were used, because `let` creates a new lexical binding per iteration.

options.text: `undefined`, `undefined`, `undefined`
options.explanation: `i` remains accessible in scope with value 3.
`i` was incremented to 3 before timers executed.

questions.body: How does JavaScript resolve an identifier name that is not declared in the local function scope?
questions.keyPoints: Traverses upwards through parent lexical environments until global scope.

options.text: It traverses outward through nesting lexical parent environments until reaching global scope; if not found, it throws a ReferenceError.
options.explanation: Identifier lookup follows the static lexical scope chain upwards to outer functions and eventually global scope.

options.text: It searches the call stack at runtime to find where the function was called from.
options.explanation: JavaScript uses static lexical scoping, not dynamic scoping based on the call stack.

options.text: It searches the prototype chain of the function object itself.
options.explanation: Variable resolution checks lexical environments, not object prototype chains.

options.text: It automatically creates a local variable initialized to `undefined`.
options.explanation: In strict mode or reading access, an undeclared variable throws ReferenceError.

questions.body: What is the difference between function declarations and function expressions regarding hoisting?
questions.keyPoints: Function declarations are hoisted with their definitions; function expressions only have their variable hoisted.

options.text: Function declarations are hoisted entirely with their implementation, while function expressions are subject to variable hoisting rules (e.g. `undefined` for `var`).
options.explanation: `function foo() {}` is completely hoisted and callable before its line of declaration. `var foo = function() {}` has only variable `foo` hoisted as `undefined`, causing `TypeError: foo is not a function` if called beforehand.

options.text: Function expressions are hoisted with full body, while function declarations are not hoisted at all.
options.explanation: The opposite is true.

options.text: Both are hoisted with their implementations identically.
options.explanation: Function expressions assign functions to variables at runtime evaluation.

options.text: Neither is hoisted in strict mode.
options.explanation: Hoisting rules still apply in strict mode.

questions.body: Which declaration keywords in JavaScript create block-scoped bindings?
questions.keyPoints: let and const are block scoped; var is function/global scoped.

options.text: `let` and `const`
options.explanation: `let` and `const` bind variables to the nearest enclosing pair of curly braces `{}` (if, for, while, or bare block). `var` binds to the nearest enclosing function.

options.text: `var`, `let`, and `const`
options.explanation: `var` is function-scoped, ignoring bare blocks.

options.text: `var` only
options.explanation: `var` is explicitly not block-scoped.

options.text: `function` and `var`
options.explanation: `var` is function-scoped.

questions.body: How can unexpected closures cause memory leaks in single-page web applications?
questions.keyPoints: Inner functions retain references to outer scope variables preventing garbage collection.

options.text: Long-lived closures (like event listeners or timers) retain references to large outer variables or DOM elements, preventing them from being garbage collected.
options.explanation: If a closure attaches to an active event listener or interval, everything retained in its lexical environment record stays in memory, preventing GC of outer objects and DOM elements.

options.text: Closures duplicate the entire JavaScript engine heap per invocation.
options.explanation: Closures do not clone the engine heap; they maintain environment record pointers.

options.text: Closures bypass the browser's mark-and-sweep garbage collector completely.
options.explanation: Mark-and-sweep processes them normally; the problem is valid reachability prevents collection.

options.text: Closures continuously allocate stack memory indefinitely.
options.explanation: Closures reside in heap memory once the stack frame returns.

questions.body: What functional programming technique transforms a function `f(a, b, c)` into callable sequence `f(a)(b)(c)` using closures?
questions.keyPoints: Currying transforms a multi-argument function into a chain of single-argument functions.

options.text: Currying
options.explanation: Currying converts a function with multiple arguments into a chain of functions each taking one argument, utilizing closures to store accumulated arguments.

options.text: Memoization
options.explanation: Memoization is caching function outputs based on input arguments.

options.text: Debouncing
options.explanation: Debouncing limits the rate at which a function fires.

options.text: Throttling
options.explanation: Throttling enforces a maximum number of executions over a given time interval.

questions.body: How is a closure typically utilized to implement a `memoize` higher-order function?
questions.keyPoints: Outer function holds a cache object; returned inner function checks cache before computation.

options.text: The outer function maintains a `cache` object in its lexical scope, which the returned wrapper function reads from and writes to across calls.
options.explanation: The returned inner function forms a closure over the `cache` map/object created in the outer scope, preserving cached results across invocations.

options.text: It stores results in `window.localStorage` automatically.
options.explanation: Memoization is in-memory caching via local scope closures.

options.text: It attaches cache entries directly to the function prototype property.
options.explanation: Closures encapsulate private caches without polluting prototypes.

options.text: It freezes the input arguments using `Object.freeze`.
options.explanation: Memoization tracks outputs for inputs, it does not freeze inputs.

questions.body: Before ES modules existed, how did the IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) Module Pattern achieve private state in JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: Private variables live in the IIFE function scope; public methods are returned as an object.

options.text: Variables declared inside the IIFE remained private to its function scope, while exposing only selected methods in a returned object.
options.explanation: The IIFE creates private scope for variables. The returned object contains closure methods that access and manipulate the private variables.

options.text: By prefixing private variables with `#`.
options.explanation: `#` private fields were introduced in modern ES2022 classes, long after the IIFE pattern.

options.text: By executing the code in a Web Worker thread.
options.explanation: Module pattern runs in the main thread using standard lexical scoping.

options.text: By freezing the global `window` object.
options.explanation: Global object freezing would break third-party libraries and page scripts.

questions.body: In strict mode (`'use strict'`), what happens to variables declared inside an `eval()` string?
questions.keyPoints: In strict mode, eval has its own lexical scope and cannot inject variables into the calling environment.

options.text: `eval()` creates its own private scope; variables declared inside do not leak into the calling scope.
options.explanation: In non-strict mode, direct `eval('var x = 1')` creates `x` in the surrounding scope. In strict mode, `eval` has its own isolated scope.

options.text: Variables are hoisted to the enclosing function's top scope normally.
options.explanation: Strict mode prevents `eval` from mutating enclosing environment records.

options.text: Variables become properties of the global `window` object.
options.explanation: They do not leak globally.

options.text: Calling `eval` in strict mode throws a SyntaxError immediately.
options.explanation: Eval is allowed in strict mode (though discouraged), but executes in a sandbox scope.

questions.body: In non-strict mode, what happens when an assignment is made to an undeclared variable (e.g. `foo = 42`) inside a function?
questions.keyPoints: In sloppy mode, assigning to undeclared variable creates an implicit global property.

options.text: It creates a new property on the global object (`window.foo = 42`), polluting global scope.
options.explanation: In non-strict mode, assigning to an unresolved identifier creates an implicit global variable. In strict mode, it throws a `ReferenceError`.

options.text: It throws a ReferenceError immediately.
options.explanation: ReferenceError is thrown in strict mode; non-strict creates an implicit global.

options.text: It creates a local variable scoped only to that function.
options.explanation: Without `var`, `let`, or `const`, it navigates all scopes up to global and assigns to global.

options.text: The assignment is silently ignored.
options.explanation: The global variable is actively created.

questions.body: What is variable shadowing in JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: An inner scope variable declares the same identifier name as an outer scope variable.

options.text: When a variable declared in an inner scope has the exact same name as a variable in an outer scope, masking access to the outer variable.
options.explanation: Variable shadowing occurs when an inner identifier takes precedence over an outer identifier of the same name within the inner block/function.

options.text: When a variable value is rendered invisible to CSS stylesheets.
options.explanation: CSS has nothing to do with JS lexical identifier shadowing.

options.text: When two asynchronous tasks overwrite the same shared object property.
options.explanation: That describes a race condition.

options.text: When a variable cannot be reassigned due to `const`.
options.explanation: That is immutability of bindings, not shadowing.

questions.body: According to the ECMAScript specification, what two key components make up an Execution Context?
questions.keyPoints: LexicalEnvironment, VariableEnvironment, and this binding / code evaluation state.

options.text: LexicalEnvironment and VariableEnvironment (along with ThisBinding and code evaluation state).
options.explanation: An execution context contains a LexicalEnvironment (resolves let/const and outer references), a VariableEnvironment (resolves var/functions), and this/evaluation tracking state.

options.text: Call Stack and Event Loop.
options.explanation: Call Stack and Event Loop are runtime concurrency architecture mechanisms.

options.text: Heap Memory and Garbage Collector.
options.explanation: Those are memory management subsystems.

options.text: DOM Tree and CSSOM Tree.
options.explanation: Those are browser rendering engine document structures.

questions.body: In ES6, where do function default parameter expressions execute in relation to the function body scope?
questions.keyPoints: Default parameters execute in their own intermediate parameter scope between parent and body.

options.text: In a separate intermediate parameter scope that sits between the outer scope and the function body scope.
options.explanation: ES6 default parameters create an intermediate scope. Expressions inside parameter defaults cannot see variables declared inside the function body.

options.text: Directly inside the function body scope.
options.explanation: Parameters cannot reference variables declared inside the body with `let`/`const`.

options.text: In the global scope unconditionally.
options.explanation: Parameter scope has access to outer enclosing scopes, not just global.

options.text: Inside the caller's execution context.
options.explanation: They are evaluated when entering the callee context.

questions.body: How did developers implement truly private instance data before native `#privateField` syntax?
questions.keyPoints: Storing private state in a module-scoped WeakMap keyed by the instance `this`.

options.text: By storing private data in a module-scoped `WeakMap` with `this` (the instance) as the key.
options.explanation: Because `WeakMap` keys are weak references, when the instance is garbage collected, its private data in the WeakMap is automatically cleared, without exposing properties on the object.

options.text: By prefixing property names with an underscore `_`.
options.explanation: Underscore prefix is purely an informal naming convention; properties remain fully public.

options.text: By deleting the properties inside the constructor after initialization.
options.explanation: Deleting properties would remove the state entirely, rendering methods unusable.

options.text: By defining classes inside WebAssembly binaries.
options.explanation: Not a standard or practical JS pattern.

questions.body: Why is it important to remove event listeners that close over components when components unmount in modern web apps?
questions.keyPoints: Dangling event listeners prevent garbage collection of closed-over components and DOM references.

options.text: Because the window or document retains the listener callback, which holds references to the unmounted component in its closure, causing memory leaks.
options.explanation: The global event target keeps the callback alive. The callback's closure keeps the component's state, props, and DOM nodes reachable, preventing garbage collection.

options.text: Because the browser will automatically crash after 10 unmounted listeners.
options.explanation: There is no hard limit; memory grows silently until performance degrades.

options.text: Because removing listeners is required to trigger DOM reflows.
options.explanation: Reflows are triggered by style/layout mutations, not listener removal.

options.text: Because unmounted event listeners automatically throw UnhandledRejection errors.
options.explanation: Listeners continue running silently on events unless removed.

questions.body: What scope is created by the `catch (err)` clause of a `try...catch` statement?
questions.keyPoints: The catch clause creates a block scope where the error identifier err is bound locally.

options.text: A block scope specifically for the error parameter `err` and statements inside `{}`.
options.explanation: The `catch (err)` clause creates a block scope where the error variable is bound locally. In modern JS, omitted catch binding `catch { ... }` is also supported.

options.text: A new function scope that requires an explicit `return`.
options.explanation: It is a block scope, not a function scope.

options.text: No scope; `err` is hoisted into the outer function scope like `var`.
options.explanation: `err` is block-scoped to the catch clause.

options.text: A global scope property.
options.explanation: It does not leak globally.

questions.body: What is the key conceptual distinction between Partial Application and Currying?
questions.keyPoints: Partial application fixes a number of arguments returning a function of lower arity; currying produces a chain of single-argument functions.

options.text: Partial application fixes a subset of arguments returning a function expecting the rest, whereas Currying produces a chain of unary (single-argument) functions.
options.explanation: Partial application takes a function of arity N and fixes K arguments to return a function of arity (N-K). Currying specifically produces unary functions: `f(a)(b)(c)`.

options.text: Partial application only works with async functions.
options.explanation: Both apply to synchronous and asynchronous functions alike.

options.text: Currying mutates the original function while partial application does not.
options.explanation: Both are pure functional patterns that return new functions.

options.text: There is no difference; they are exact synonyms in computer science.
options.explanation: They are related but distinct concepts regarding arity.

questions.subtopic: Shared Variable Mutation in Multiple Closures
questions.keyPoints: All methods returned from createCounters share the exact same count variable in their closure.

options.text: `1`, because all three methods close over the same shared mutable `count` variable in memory.
options.explanation: The three inner arrow functions share the identical lexical environment binding `count`. Incrementing twice and decrementing once leaves `count` at 1.

options.text: `0`, because arrow functions copy primitive values by value into their own scopes.
options.explanation: Closures retain references to the environment record variable, not static value copies.

options.text: `NaN`, because `count` cannot be shared across multiple functions.
options.explanation: Sharing variables across closure methods is standard JS behavior.

options.text: `2`, because `dec()` creates a separate variable instance.
options.explanation: Both mutate the single shared `count` binding.
